nodes.name: Theorem 2.1 (Uniqueness)
nodes.statement: Let $T>0$ and let conditions {\rm(i)--(ii)} on $\beta$ and $b$ hold. For each $u_0\in L^\9\cap L^1$, the \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd). \end{equation}
assumptions: Let $T>0$ and let conditions {\rm(i)--(ii)} on $\beta$ and $b$ hold.
conclusions: the \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At most one distributional solution in $L^1\cap L^\infty$ to the FP equation, under (i)-(ii).
nodes.label: t1

nodes.name: Theorem 2.4 (Existence and uniqueness)
nodes.statement: Under hypotheses {\rm(i), (ii), (ii'), (iii)}, for each $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\9$, equation \eqref{e1.1} has a unique distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd),\ \ff T>0. \end{equation}
conclusions: equation \eqref{e1.1} has a unique distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd),\ \ff T>0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Existence and uniqueness of a distributional solution under the full hypothesis set (i),(ii),(ii'),(iii).
nodes.label: t4

nodes.name: Proposition 2.3 (Boundedness of the mild solution)
nodes.statement: Assume that {\rm (i), (ii), (ii')} hold, and that, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u$, \begin{itemize} \item[{\rm(iii)}] $\Phi\in C^2(\rrd).$ \end{itemize} Then, for each $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\9$, the mild solution $u$ to \eqref{e1.1} satisfies also \begin{equation} u\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd),\ \ff T>0. \end{equation}
assumptions: Assume that {\rm (i), (ii), (ii')} hold, and that, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u$, \begin{itemize} \item[{\rm(iii)}] $\Phi\in C^2(\rrd).$ \end{itemize}
conclusions: the mild solution $u$ to \eqref{e1.1} satisfies also \begin{equation} u\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd),\ \ff T>0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The mild solution stays in $L^\infty$ for all time, under (i),(ii),(ii'),(iii).
nodes.label: p2

nodes.name: Claim 2.2
nodes.statement: If $u$ is a distributional solution to \eqref{e1.1} satisfying \eqref{add-e5}, then \eqref{add-e6} holds.
assumptions: $u$ is a distributional solution to \eqref{e1.1} satisfying \eqref{add-e5}
nodes.statement_short: Any distributional solution satisfying (add-e5) automatically has the extra Sobolev regularity (add-e6).
nodes.label: add-l1

nodes.name: Theorem 3.1 (Linearized uniqueness)
nodes.statement: {\bf(Linearized uniqueness)} Under hypotheses {\rm(i)--(ii)}, for each $v_0\in L^1\cap L^\9$ and $T>0$, equation \eqref{e3.1} has at most one distributional solution $v\in L^{1}([0,T];L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).$
conclusions: equation \eqref{e3.1} has at most one distributional solution $v\in L^{1}([0,T];L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).$
nodes.statement_short: At most one distributional solution to the linearized FP equation, by the Theorem 2.1 energy argument.
nodes.label: t5

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1 (Weak uniqueness for the McKean-Vlasov SDE)
nodes.statement: Let $0<T<\9$ and let the above conditions {\rm(i)--(ii)} on $b$ and $\b$ hold. Let $X(t)$, $t\ge0$, and $\wt X(t),$ $t\ge0$, be two solutions to \eqref{e4.1} such that,~for $$u(t,\cdot):=\frac{d\mathcal{L}_{X(t)}}{dx},\ \ \wt u(t,\cdot):=\frac{d\mathcal{L}_{\wt X(t)}}{dx},$$we have \begin{equation} u,\wt u\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).\end{equation}Then $X$ and $\wt X$ have the same laws, i.e., $\mathbb{P}\circ X\1=\mathbb{P}\circ\wt X^{-1}.$

nodes.name: Existence of the mild solution (Barbu-Rockner 2019)
nodes.statement: In \cite{1} it was proved, in particular, that, if (i)--(ii) hold and, in addition, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr,$ we have $\Phi\in C^2(\rr)$, then there is a mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1(\rr^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1(\rr^d)$.

assumptions: if (i)--(ii) hold and, in addition, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr,$ we have $\Phi\in C^2(\rr)$

nodes.name: Mild solution (via implicit Euler scheme)
nodes.statement: The mild solution $u$ is defined~as $$u(t)=\lim_{h\to0}u_h(t)\mbox{ in }L^1(\rr^d),\ \ff t\ge0,$$where \begin{equation} \label{e1.6} \barr{l} u_h(t)=u^i_h\mbox{ for }t\in[ih,(i+h)h],\ i=0,1,...,Nh=T,\vsp u^{i+1}_h-h\D\b(u^{i+1}_h)+h\,{\rm div}(b(x,u^{i+1}_h)u^{i+1}_h)=u^i_h\mbox{ in }\cald'(\rr^d),\\\hfill i=0,1,...,\vsp u^0_h=u_0.\earr \end{equation}Moreover, $S(t)u_0=u(t),\ t\ge0,$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1(\rrd)$.
nodes.statement_short: The mild solution is the $L^1$-limit of the implicit-Euler scheme $u_h$; $S(t)u_0:=u(t)$ is a nonexpansive semigroup.

nodes.name: Any mild solution is a distributional solution
nodes.statement: As easily seen, any mild solution is a distributional solution but the uniqueness follows in the class of mild solutions only.

nodes.name: Notation: function spaces and pairings
nodes.statement: \n{\bf Notation.} Denote by $L^p(\rr^d)=L^p$ the space of $p$-summable functions on $L^p$, with the norm denoted $|\cdot|_p$. By $H^k(\rrd)=H^k$, $k=1,2$, and $H^{-k}(\rrd)=H^{-k},$ we denote the standard Sobolev spaces on $\rrd$ and by $C_b(\rrd)$ the space of continuous and bounded functions on $\rrd$. By $C^k(\rrd)$ we denote the space of continuously differentiable functions on $\rrd$ of order $k$, by $C^1_b(\rrd)$ the space $\left\{u\in C^1(\rrd);\frac{\pp u}{\pp y}\in C_b(\rrd),\ j=1,...,d\right\}.$ The spaces of continuous and differentiable functions on $(0,T)\times\rrd$ are denoted in a similar way and we shall simply write $$C^1_b(\rrd)=C^1_b,\ C^k(\rrd)=C^k,\ k=1,2.$$ The scalar product in $L^2$ is denoted $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_2$ and by ${}_{H^{-1}}\!\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{H^1}$ the pairing between $H^1$ and $H^{-1}.$ Of course, on $L^2\times L^2$ this coincides with $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_2.$ The~scalar product $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{-1}$ on $H\1$ is taken~as \begin{equation} \label{e1.8} \<u,v\>_{-1}=\<(I-\D)\1u,v\>_2,\ \ff u,v\in H\1 \end{equation}with the corresponding norm \begin{equation} \label{e1.9} |u|_{-1}=(\<u,u\>_{-1})^{\frac12},\ u\in H\1. \end{equation} By $\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)$ and $\cald'(\rrd)$ we denote the space of Schwartz distributions on $(0,\9)\times\rrd$ and $\rrd$, respectively. If $\calx$ is a Banach space, we denote by $W^{1,2}([0,T];\calx)$ the infinite dimensional Sobolev space $\{y\in L^2(0,T;\calx);$ $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;\calx)\}$, where $\frac d{dt}$ is taken in the sense of vectorial distributions. We also set, for each $z\in C^1(\rrd\times\rr)$, $$z_r(x,r)=\frac\pp{\pp r}\ z(x,r),\ \ z_x=\nabla_x z(x,r).$$ We shall denote the norms on $\rrd$ and $\rr$ by the same symbol $|\cdot|$.
nodes.statement_short: Standard notation for $L^p$, Sobolev spaces $H^k$, and the $L^2$/$H^1$-$H^{-1}$ pairings used throughout.

nodes.name: Standing hypotheses (i), (ii), (ii') on $\beta$ and $b$
nodes.statement: where $\b:\rr\to\rr$ and $b:\rrd\times\rr\to\rrd$ satisfy the following assumptions \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] {\it$\beta(0)=0$, $\b\in C^1(\rr)$, and \begin{equation} \g_0|r_1-r_2|^2\le(\b(r_1)-\b(r_2))(r_1-r_2),\ r_1,r_2\in\rr,\label{e1.2} \end{equation} where $0<\g_0<\9.$ } \item[(ii)] $b\in C_b(\mathbb R^{d+1}; \rrd)$, $b(x, \cdot) \in C^1(\rrd; \rrd)$ $ \forall x\in\rrd$ {\it such that} $$\mbox{$\sup\{|b^i_r(x,r)|;x\in\rrd,i=1,2,$ $|r|\le M\}\le C_M,$ $\ff M>0.$}$$ \item[(ii')] $b(x,0)=0$ $\forall x\in\rrd$, $b \in C^1(\mathbb R^{d+1}; \rrd) $ {\it and for $$\delta(r):=\sup\{|b_x(x,r)|;\ x\in\rrd\},$$we have} $\delta\in C_b(\rr).$ \end{itemize} Here$$b(x,u)=\{b^i(x,u)\}^d_{i=1}\mbox{ and }b^i_r=\frac{\pp b^i}{\pp r}, b_x=\big\{ \nabla_x \, b^i(x, \cdot) \big\}_{i=1}^d.$$

nodes.statement: In the special case $b\equiv0$, such a uniqueness result for\eqref{e1.1} was established earlier in \cite{3} for continuous and monotonically nondecreasing functions $\b$.

conclusions: such a uniqueness result for\eqref{e1.1} was established earlier in \cite{3} for continuous and monotonically nondecreasing functions $\b$.

Furthermore, again by It\^o's formula, $\mathbb{P}\circ X\1$ and $\mathbb{P}\circ\wt X\1$ satisfy the martingale problem with the initial condition $u_0dx$ for the linear Komogorov operator $$L_u:=\Phi(u)\D+b(\cdot,u)\cdot\nabla,$$where $\Phi(u)=\frac{\b(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr.$ Hence, by Theorem \ref{t5}, the assertion follows by Lemma 2.12 in \cite{4}. Here, for $s\in[0,T]$, the set $\mathcal{R}_{[s,T]}$, which appears in that lemma, is chosen to be the set of all narrowly continuous, probability measure-valued solutions of \eqref{e3.1} having for each $t\in[s,T]$ a density \mbox{$v(t,\cdot)\in L^\9$} with respect to Lebesgue measure such that \mbox{$v\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).$}

nodes.statement_short: Transfers uniqueness from Theorem 2.1/3.1 to the SDE's law via the Fokker-Planck/martingale-problem correspondence and a cited well-posedness lemma (Trevisan 2016).

nodes.name: Solution process (to the McKean-Vlasov SDE)
nodes.statement: Consider for $T\in(0,\9)$ and $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\9$ the McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equation (SDE) \begin{equation}\label{e4.1} \barr{l} dX(t)=b(X(t),u(t,X(t)))dt +\dd\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\(\frac{\b(u(t,X(t)))}{u(t,X(t))}\)^{\frac12}dW(t),\vsp \hfill 0\le t\le T,\\ u(0,\cdot)=\xi_0,\earr\end{equation}on $\rrd$. Here, $W(t),\ t\ge0,$ is an $(\calf_t)$-Brownian motion on a probability space $(\Omega,\calf,\mathbb{P})$ with normal filtration $\calf_t$, $t\ge0,$ $\xi_0:\Omega\to\rrd$ is $\calf_0$-measurable such that $$\mathbb{P}\circ\xi^{-1}_0(dx)=u_0(x)dx,$$ and $u(t,x)=\frac{d\mathcal{L}_{X(t)}}{dx}\,(x)$ is the Lebesgue density of the marginal law $\mathcal{L}_{X(t)}=\mathbb{P}\circ X(t)\1$ of the solution process $X(t)$, $t\ge0$. Here, a solution process means an $(\calf_t)$-adapted process with $\pas$ continuous sample paths in $\rrd$ solving \eqref{e4.1}.
